learn.title: Iron-Air Batteries for Long-Duration Storage
learn.intro: Iron-air batteries store energy for 100+ hours using abundant materials like iron and oxygen, addressing solar/wind intermittency. They offer low-cost, scalable solutions for grid stability, crucial for India's 500 GW renewable target by 2030. These batteries enable seasonal storage, reducing reliance on fossil backups.
learn.c1_text: During charging, iron oxidizes at the anode while oxygen from air reduces at the cathode. Energy is stored chemically, with iron reversing during discharge. Unlike lithium-ion, they use cheap, non-toxic materials. A 100 MWh system could power 10,000 homes for 10 hours, scaling to weeks.
learn.c2_text: Iron-air batteries cost ~$50/kWh, 10x cheaper than lithium-ion. Their modular design allows gigawatt-scale deployment. For India, this means affordable storage for remote villages and industrial parks, complementing solar projects like Gujarat's 2.8 GW plant.
learn.c3_text: India aims for 500 GW renewables by 2030, requiring 200 GWh storage. Iron-air could store monsoon surplus solar for winter. States like Rajasthan are testing hybrid solar-storage projects. The National Energy Storage Mission prioritizes long-duration tech for rural electrification.

learn.title: Capacity Factor Explained
learn.intro: Capacity factor measures actual energy output vs. maximum possible, revealing real-world performance. Solar/wind often lag behind fossil plants due to weather dependency. For India's grid, understanding this gap is vital for planning 500 GW renewables and avoiding curtailment of 10% of wind/solar output.
learn.c1_text: Capacity factor = (actual output / max output) × 100. A 100 MW solar plant with 25% capacity factor produces 60 GWh/year (25 MW average). Fossil plants achieve 80-90% due to constant operation, while solar peaks at noon, wind varies with speed.
learn.c2_text: Solar capacity factors range from 15-30% depending on location and cloud cover. India's Rajasthan solar farms achieve 28%, while Himalayan regions drop to 18%. Wind farms in Gujarat hit 40%, while coastal sites reach 50%. This affects grid planning and pricing.
learn.c3_text: India's renewable share rose to 30% in 2023 but faces curtailment. Solar capacity factor drops to 15% in cloudy months. The government mandates 20% storage for new projects to address variability. States like Tamil Nadu lose 12% of solar output to grid constraints.
learn.readLabel: Read at US Energy Info Admin

learn.title: Green Hydrogen via Water Electrolysis
learn.intro: Green hydrogen produces clean fuel via water splitting using renewable electricity. India's National Green Hydrogen Mission targets 5 MT/year by 2030. Choosing between PEM and alkaline electrolyzers depends on cost, efficiency, and application needs, from steelmaking to fertilizer production.
learn.c1_text: PEM uses a solid polymer membrane, enabling fast response and high efficiency (70-80%). Alkaline uses liquid KOH electrolyte, cheaper but slower. PEM suits variable solar power, while alkaline works for steady steam methane reforming replacements in ammonia plants.
learn.c2_text: PEM electrolyzers convert 70-80% of renewable electricity to hydrogen, with lower water usage. Alkaline achieves 60-70% efficiency but requires high-pressure systems. For India, PEM could power hydrogen fuel cells in trucks, while alkaline supports green fertilizer production in Punjab's ammonia plants.
learn.c3_text: India's $2.5 billion green hydrogen subsidies aim to cut electrolyzer costs by 40% by 2030. Gujarat's Adani Green Hydrogen plant (1,000 tons/year) uses alkaline tech. The mission targets 500 electrolyzer units by 2030, creating 100,000 jobs in solar-hydrogen corridors.

learn.title: Solid-State Batteries: Safety and Energy Density
learn.intro: Solid-state batteries replace flammable liquid electrolytes with ceramics, polymers, or glass, boosting safety and energy density to 500 Wh/kg. For India's EV push, this means 1,000 km range for electric trucks and safer home storage. Companies like Tata and ABB are investing in this technology.
learn.c1_text: They use solid electrolytes like sulfides or oxides, eliminating fire risks. Energy density reaches 500 Wh/kg vs 250 Wh/kg for lithium-ion. A 100 kWh solid-state pack weighs half as much, enabling 800 km EV range. Toyota's prototype achieves 1,000 km in lab tests.
learn.c2_text: Production requires high-temperature sintering, increasing costs to $150/kWh (vs $100 for lithium-ion). Interface stability between solid electrolytes and electrodes is critical. For India, partnerships with Japan/South Korea are key to scaling up, as local supply chains need 5-10 years to mature.
learn.c3_text: India's PLI scheme offers $2.5 billion subsidies for lithium-ion gigafactories. Solid-state adoption could leapfrog this, with Tata Motors testing prototypes for buses. The National EV Policy aims for 30% electric sales by 2030, requiring battery innovations for Indian heat and dust conditions.

learn.title: Microgrids for Energy Independence
learn.intro: Microgrids are localized grids combining renewables, storage, and loads, ensuring energy independence for villages and resilience during disasters. India's Saubhagya scheme targets 90% household electrification, with microgrids powering remote areas. Post-disaster, they restore power faster than centralized grids.
learn.c1_text: A microgrid includes solar/wind, batteries, and smart controllers, managing supply/demand locally. A 1 MW solar microgrid with 2 MWh storage can power 500 homes and a school. During grid outages, it operates autonomously, reducing blackout risks by 70% in rural areas.
learn.c2_text: Advanced microgrids use AI for demand prediction and fault detection. After Cyclone Amphan (2020), microgrids in West Bengal restored power in 48 hours vs 10 days for the main grid. Blockchain enables peer-to-peer energy trading, as tested in Kerala's solar microgrid villages.
learn.c3_text: India has 1,000 microgrids under the Ministry of Power, with 500 in Arunachal Pradesh and Sikkim. The 2023 National Microgrid Policy offers 30% capital subsidy. Projects like Delhi's 100 MW solar microgrid for rural schools aim to electrify 10,000 villages by 2030, aligning with SDGs.
learn.stat2: Disaster recovery time: 48 hours vs 10 days

learn.title: Pumped Hydro Storage: World's Largest Battery
learn.intro: Pumped hydro storage (PHS) uses gravity, pumping water uphill to generate electricity when needed. It provides 90% of global long-duration storage. India's first PHS plant (200 MW, Chamera) supports hydropower integration. With 40 GW global capacity, it's key for balancing India's 500 GW renewable mix.
learn.c1_text: During low demand, excess power pumps water from lower to upper reservoir. When needed, water flows down through turbines to generate electricity—4-8 hours of storage per cycle. A 1,000 MW PHS plant stores 4,000 MWh, enough for 1 million homes for 4 hours.
learn.c2_text: Global PHS capacity: 165 GW, with 250 GW potential. India has 50 GW technical potential, mainly in Himalayan states. The 1,000 MW Koyna PHS project in Maharashtra will store 4,000 MWh, supporting 2,000 MW solar integration. New projects use closed-loop systems to minimize environmental impact.
learn.c3_text: India's 14 PHS plants total 3.5 GW, with 12 under construction. The 1,000 MW Srisailam project (AP) will store 4,000 MWh, aiding 2,000 MW solar. The National Hydroelectric Power Corporation aims for 10 GW by 2030. PHS complements solar in Rajasthan's 10 GW solar park, using excess power for pumping.
learn.stat3: Pumped hydro storage: 90% of global long-duration
